headline: High: shared project-directory writes plus MCP/API bridging create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risks; compliance risk is medium.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A writes files in a shared project directory and has no self-isolation by default; Agent B can connect via MCP/API and may ingest those files or outputs as context. That creates a realistic instruction-hijack path from A’s generated code/comments into B’s planning flow. The interaction is documented by both profiles, though the exact parser behavior is not.
conditions: IF Agent B reads project files or MCP-fed content as instructions without provenance filtering, injection is possible.
IF Agent A writes attacker-controlled text into the shared project directory, B can be steered.
mitigations: Add a provenance banner to all A-generated files before B reads them.
Disable MCP ingestion of untrusted project files for B.
Review A outputs in a separate scratch directory first.
Require B to treat file contents as data unless explicitly promoted.
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance tracking between the agents.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A has broad filesystem read/write and broad network egress, while Agent B touches long-term user facts and conversational context and can call APIs/MCP. If they share the project directory, A can read B-produced artifacts and B can transmit sensitive context outward. The profiles show a plausible shared-workspace path, but not direct evidence of automatic secret exposure.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same project directory, A can read B artifacts.
IF B forwards conversational context through MCP/API, sensitive user facts can leave the local workspace.
mitigations: Separate A and B into different directories.
Turn off B MCP access for sensitive sessions.
Redact user facts before passing text from B to A.
Audit outbound requests from A and B for sensitive strings.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent workspace ACLs.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses; B can use MCP and network egress. Even though A does not modify git state, both can mutate shared project artifacts and external services without an explicit locking primitive in either profile. That overlap can cause conflicting writes or duplicated side effects in default project-directory workflows.
conditions: IF both agents target the same project directory, concurrent writes can collide.
IF B uses MCP to mutate shared resources while A edits files, state divergence can occur.
mitigations: Run only one agent at a time on a shared workspace.
Use separate branches or directories per agent.
Add a manual lock file before edits.
Check diffs before applying either agent’s changes.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces generated source code and can execute generated code; B handles travel-planning context and can act through MCP/API. If B treats A’s code or textual output as authoritative, an error in A can cascade into incorrect downstream actions or plans. The pair lacks a documented verification barrier, so the safer choice is the higher severity.
conditions: IF B consumes A output without independent verification, errors propagate.
IF A-generated code is executed or reused by B, downstream actions can be wrong or unsafe.
mitigations: Require B to verify A outputs against source data.
Keep A outputs as drafts until human review.
Block direct execution of A-generated code by B.
Add a checklist for factual claims before B acts.
requires-engineering: implement automated validation gates.

E_compliance.rationale: A handles generated source code and OPENAI_API_KEY, while B handles long-term user facts and conversational context. The profiles do not show a residency mismatch or regulated-data certification gap, so this is not high. However, differing retention and logging expectations across a coding agent and a memory-backed travel agent create a plausible compliance mismatch in default use.
conditions: IF either agent retains prompts or outputs longer than the other, retention policy mismatch occurs.
IF user facts from B are copied into A logs or code artifacts, subject-rights handling becomes harder.
mitigations: Avoid placing personal data into A’s project files.
Set short retention on B logs for sensitive sessions.
Document which agent stores which data class.
Delete temporary artifacts after handoff.
requires-engineering: align retention and deletion workflows.
